description_full: The Marcus Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, owns and operates movie theatres, and hotels and resorts in the United States. The company operates a family entertainment center and multiscreen motion picture theatres under the Marcus Theatres, Movie Tavern by Marcus, and BistroPlex brand names. It also owns and operates full-service hotels and resorts, as well as manages full-service hotels, resorts, and other properties. In addition, the company provides hospitality management services, including check-in, housekeeping, and maintenance for vacation ownership development; manages condominium hotels under management contracts; and commercial laundry services. The Marcus Corporation was founded in 1935 and is headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

financial_summary: Marcus Corporation (The) is a small-cap communication services business with a $838M market cap on $758M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 2% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $989,000 in free cash flow — roughly 0 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 6.63× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.6× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 1.5× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.1%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 7.1% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 2% operating margin trails the Communication Services median (9%) by 6pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.11x its revenue share).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 171 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 81% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 9% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 17% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 37% and a beta of 0.75, it is more defensive than the market.
About $5.7M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 77% in the 2020 crash, 28% in the 2022 bear market and 65% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $8.63 (margin of safety -212%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 5%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $5.24 to $13.85 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: P/E 32.9 vs 15.4 and P/FCF 847.2 vs 11.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 270% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 0.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 4 covering analysts target $32.50 on average, 21% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 2% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.90).
It converts 0% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 3% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 5pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 1.0% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.6x net debt to EBITDA ($23.4M of cash against $159.0M of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 1.5x.
The current ratio of 0.40 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.8% over 3 years, 26.1% over 5 years and 4.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 34%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.2x, 11.0% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 25, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 26.7% on average.
own: Insiders own 7.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 89%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 5 sales over the past year, net $2.0M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.1% (1.3% in dividends).
people: With about 2,349 employees, each generates about $323K of revenue, 0.5x the Communication Services median, and revenue has grown 4.8% a year across its filed history.
CEO pay is $2.2M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
